title: She Survived the Titanic. And Both of Its Sister Ships #shorts
description:
Case 012. Violet Jessop was a ship's stewardess. In 1911 she was working aboard the liner Olympic when it collided with the warship HMS Hawke; the Olympic was torn open below the waterline and limped back to port. In 1912 she joined the Olympic's sister ship, the Titanic; when it struck an iceberg she was put into a lifeboat, and by her account a baby was thrust into her arms as it was lowered. In 1916 she was serving with the British Red Cross aboard the third sister, Britannic, by then a hospital ship, when it struck a mine in the Aegean Sea. She had complained after the Titanic about losing her toothbrush, so this time she took it. The ship's propellers were still turning as it went down and they pulled lifeboats in. She jumped, and came out of the water with a fractured skull. She recovered, went back to sea and worked on ships until 1950. She died in 1971. Rook didn't believe it either.

Animated reconstruction of a true story. The ships, quay, cabin and coastlines in the film are generic low-poly sets, not models of the real vessels or places, and the cards and lists are drawings made for it, not real documents. Many people died in the Titanic and Britannic sinkings; the film shows neither.

source_notes: Read for this run (fetched 14 Nov 2026): History.co.uk ('The unsinkable Violet Jessop', BP Perry); Mental Floss ('The Unsinkable Violet Jessop', Stacy Conradt, 2015); National Geographic (David Kindy, March 2023). Wikipedia, Encyclopedia Titanica and Britannica could not be fetched in this run, so nothing in the film rests on them. Every narrated fact is in at least two of the three articles unless noted here. Agreed by all three: she was a stewardess; she was aboard the Olympic when it collided with HMS Hawke, aboard the Titanic when it sank, and aboard the Britannic when it struck a mine; at the Britannic lifeboats were pulled toward propellers that had lifted out of the sea and were still turning (History: 'pulled towards ... giant spinning propellers'; National Geographic: 'drawn into the Britannic's still-churning propellers'; Mental Floss: 'still running'), and she jumped. Two sources each: the three ships were sisters (History, National Geographic); the Britannic was a hospital ship (History, National Geographic); a baby was thrust into her arms in the Titanic lifeboat (History: by one of the ship's officers as the boat was lowered; Mental Floss: by 'someone'; the script says 'someone', the film shows a ship's officer); she took her toothbrush from the Britannic (Mental Floss: she 'remembered to grab it'; National Geographic quotes her memoir on missing a toothbrush after the Titanic and says she went back to her cabin for 'one particular personal care item'); she went back to sea and worked until 1950 (National Geographic, Mental Floss; History says she went back to work for the same line and others, no year). One source, supported by another: 'Torn open, it limps home' follows National Geographic ('a major rip below the waterline but managed to limp home'); History says 'badly damaged' and returned for extensive repairs. 'Her skull is fractured' follows National Geographic ('a severe skull fracture and deeply gashed leg'); History says 'a serious head injury'; Mental Floss says she hit her head on the ship's keel. The keel is shown for under a second (she rises toward the hull) and is not narrated. 'Third ship disaster in five years' is September 1911 to November 1916 by National Geographic's dates. Where the sources differ: (1) The baby: History says a woman later took it from her on the rescue ship and no record exists of what became of it; Mental Floss says it was reunited with its mother. The story comes from her own memoir; the film shows only the handing over and the description says 'by her account'. (2) HMS Hawke is a cruiser in National Geographic and a destroyer in History; the script says 'warship'. (3) Date of the Britannic sinking: 21 November 1916 (National Geographic) or 16 November (History); only the year is used. (4) Her rescue at the Britannic: pulled from the water after the engines were stopped (History), pulled in by people in another lifeboat (Mental Floss), later aboard a destroyer (National Geographic); the film shows a man in another boat hauling her out and the narration says only 'she lives'. (5) Her age at death: 83 (History, National Geographic) or 84 (Mental Floss); the description gives only the year, 1971. (6) Where the Olympic was repaired (Belfast or 'England'): not stated in the film. (7) National Geographic gives her retirement as 1950 and, in another sentence, as '32 years later'; the film follows the year, which Mental Floss also gives. Not confirmed by the sources read, and so shown but not narrated: which ship struck which in 1911. The film shows the cruiser's bow going into the liner's side near the stern, which is the usual account of that collision; the narration says only that the liner 'collides with a warship'. Left out on purpose: the deaths. More than 1,500 people died on the Titanic, and National Geographic describes people in the Britannic's boats being killed by the propellers. The Titanic sinking is seen from a distance with Rook's hat off and no joke; no one is shown being hurt at the propellers, and the empty boats are shown only before they reach them. Also left out: her childhood illness, her nursing, the nickname 'Miss Unsinkable' in narration, and the late-life telephone call about the baby (not in the sources read). Paraphrase, not quotation: no words are attributed to anyone. Dramatised, not reported: what the ships, deck, cabin, quay, coast and islands looked like (all generic; the liner model is one design re-dressed three times, the hospital ship is shown white with a green band and no red crosses, and no company flag, badge or name appears); the tea tray and her being on deck at the moment of the 1911 collision; her sitting on her bunk when the Titanic struck (National Geographic: she was in her berth); the tumbler on the washstand; that she stood up in the boat before jumping and how she jumped; the bandage and the boat she sits in afterwards; her walking up a gangway with a suitcase to go back to sea; her appearance and uniform; the weather and light in every scene; and everything Rook does, including the cabin key he pockets. Rook's jokes are limited to his own reactions (pointing at the toothbrush, shrugging, his hat); from the propellers to her rescue he says and does nothing funny.

quality_gate.method: 3D contact sheet reviewed in five rounds with fixes after each (round 1: the lifeboat's bottom boards stuck out through its hull and the boats floated above the sea; the propellers were too small to read; the cabin's daylight lamp pointed at the wall and burned the room out to white; the baby hand-over was staged with Violet's back to the camera; the Titanic was a speck in the lifeboat shot; Rook's head sat too low on the quay; the man hauling Violet out faced the wrong way. Round 2: a foreground propeller blade covered both faces in the lifeboat; the sign-off was shot from behind Rook in shadow; the porthole had black corners. Round 3, a full-length low-resolution rehearsal composited with captions, HUD, overlays, inserts and sound: shots did not line up with the words (the iceberg came before 'Iceberg', the jump before 'She jumps'), so the storyboard was re-cut to the word timings and two shots were added (40 shots); captions covered faces in five shots, so those cameras were re-aimed; the TRUE stamp hid Violet's face on the board and the ticks overran. Round 4, a second rehearsal: the automated gate failed four static stretches (the tea tray on deck, the damaged liner, the liner at night, the hospital ship from above), so those cameras were given real travel and two were restaged, and the gate then passed. Round 5: eighteen shots at higher resolution). The last rehearsal (216x384, 4 samples, every 3D frame) passed the automated gate locally: 40 shots, mean 1.12 s, longest 1.88 s, loudness -15.3 LUFS, voice 9.6 dB over the bed, host in 21/40 shots (52%), closest match to an earlier episode 0.77. Two small camera changes (Rook's framing at the sign-off, extra fill light on Rook on the hospital ship's deck) were made after that rehearsal and checked on stills only. Every 3D kind in the storyboard exists in world3d.SHOTS3D, every flat kind in scenes.SHOTS, HOST lists every kind where Rook is on screen and no others, no kind is used more than twice or twice in a row, and the repository tests pass. Audio was measured, not listened to. The fingerprint file the local gate wrote was deleted, not committed. The full-resolution render and the final gate run in the cloud.
